==Problem 9==
How many ordered triples of integers <imath>(x, y, z)</imath> satisfy the following system of inequalities?
<cmath>\begin{align*}
-x-y-z&\leq -2\\
-x+y+z&\leq 2\\
x-y+z&\leq 2\\
x+y-z&\leq 2
\end{align*}</cmath>
<imath>\textbf{(A)}\ 4 \qquad \textbf{(B)}\ 8 \qquad \textbf{(C)}\ 11 \qquad
\textbf{(D)}\ 15 \qquad \textbf{(E)}\ 17 \qquad </imath>

==Solution 1 (constructive counting)==
Simplifying the first inequality of the system, we have:
<cmath>
\begin{cases}
x+y+z \geq 2, \\
-x+y+z \leq 2, \\
x-y+z \leq 2, \\
x+y-z \leq 2.
\end{cases}
</cmath>
Subtracting the second inequality from the first now gives
<cmath>(x+y+z)-(-x+y+z) \geq 2-2 \iff 2x \geq 0 \iff x \geq 0,</cmath> and so by symmetry in <imath>x,y,z</imath> (i.e. similarly using the third and fourth inequalities), we also obtain <imath>y,z \geq 0</imath>. Therefore, without loss of generality, we can let
<cmath>
0 \leq x \leq y \leq z.
</cmath>
up to permutation. Also from the second inequality, we have <imath>y+z \leq 2+x</imath>, so using <imath>x \leq y</imath>, we deduce that
<cmath>
y+z \leq 2+x \leq 2+y \iff z \leq 2.
</cmath>


Hence <imath>0 \leq x \leq y \leq z \leq 2</imath>, and now we divide into the possible cases for <imath>x</imath>:

Case <imath>1</imath>: <imath>x=0</imath>.
Then the first two inequalities become
<cmath>y+z \geq 2, y+z \leq 2 \iff y+z=2,</cmath>and because we have <imath>x = 0 \leq y \leq z \leq 2</imath>, we deduce that <imath>(y,z)</imath> is either <imath>(0,2)</imath> or <imath>(1,1)</imath>.

Case <imath>2</imath>: <imath>x=1</imath>. Then we have got
<cmath>1+y+z \geq 2 \iff y+z \geq 1,\qquad -1+y+z \leq 2 \iff y+z \leq 3.</cmath> As <imath>x = 1 \leq y \leq z \leq 2</imath>, we can have <imath>(y,z) = (1,1)</imath> or <imath>(1,2)</imath>.

Case <imath>3</imath>: <imath>x=2</imath>. Then <imath>x = 2 \leq y \leq z \leq 2</imath>, so the only possible combination is already <imath>(y,z) = (2,2)</imath>. The other inequalities become
<cmath>
2+y+z \geq 2 \iff y+z \geq 0,\qquad -2+y+z \leq 2 \iff y+z \leq 4,
</cmath> which are also satisfied by <imath>(y,z) = (2,2)</imath>, meaning that <imath>(x,y,z) = (2,2,2)</imath> is indeed a valid solution.


Thus, up to permutation, the possible triples <imath>(x,y,z)</imath> are <imath>(0,0,2),\; (0,1,1),\; (1,1,1),\; (1,1,2),\; \text{and}\; (2,2,2)</imath>.

For each of these, we accordingly count the number of possible permutations (which will correspond to solutions <imath>(x,y,z)</imath> to the original system of inequalities): <cmath>\frac{3!}{2!}+\frac{3!}{2!}+\frac{3!}{3!}+\frac{3!}{2!}+\frac{3!}{3!} = 3+3+1+3+1 = \boxed{\textbf{(C)}\ 11}.</cmath>

== Solution 2 (complementary counting) ==
From Solution 1, we know that
<cmath>
0 \leq x, y, z \leq 2,
</cmath>
so since each variable has to be an integer, the number of possible ordered triples <imath>(x, y, z)</imath> with no other restrictions is simply <imath>3^3 = 27</imath>. Therefore, to find the number of solutions of the given system of inequalities, we count the number of ordered triples that are ''not'' solutions of the system and subtract these from the total of <imath>27</imath>.


Simplifying the first inequality, we obtain
<cmath>
x+y+z \geq 2,
</cmath>
which is false (under the conditions <imath>0 \leq x,y,z \leq 2</imath> that we already have from above) only if <imath>x+y+z</imath> is <imath>0</imath> or <imath>1</imath>. In the former case, there is just <imath>1</imath> possible ordered triple (namely <imath>(x,y,z) = (0,0,0)</imath>), while in the latter case, there are <imath>3</imath> possibilities (corresponding to each of the variables being <imath>1</imath> while the others are <imath>0</imath>). Hence there are <imath>1+3 = 4</imath> possible triples that make this inequality false.

Similarly, <imath>0 \leq x,y,z \leq 2</imath> gives <cmath>-x+y+z \leq 0+2+2 = 4,</cmath> and so the second inequality of the system would be false only if <imath>-x+y+z</imath> is either <imath>3</imath> or <imath>4</imath>. This implies <cmath>y+z \geq 3+x \geq 3,</cmath> giving two possible cases: 

Case <imath>1</imath>: <imath>y = z = 2</imath>.

In this case, to ensure that <imath>-x+y+z</imath> is either <imath>3</imath> or <imath>4</imath>, <imath>x</imath> can be either <imath>0</imath> or <imath>1</imath>, yielding <imath>2</imath> possibilities. Similarly, since the last two inequalities of the system are symmetric to the second one, the triples where, more generally, two of the variables are both <imath>2</imath> and the other one is <imath>0</imath> or <imath>1</imath> will all make at least one of the last three inequalities of the system false. Accordingly, we obtain a total of <imath>2 \cdot 3 = 6</imath> such ordered triples, each of which is clearly distinct from the <imath>4</imath> triples found above.

Case <imath>2</imath>: One of <imath>y</imath> or <imath>z</imath> is <imath>1</imath>, and the other is <imath>2</imath>.

In this case, we must have <imath>-x+y+z = 3</imath>, and thus <imath>x = 0</imath>. Using the symmetry of the last three inequalities of the system as in Case <imath>1</imath>, we similarly deduce that at least one of these inequalities will be false when the variables are <imath>0,1,2</imath> in some order. This gives <imath>3! = 6</imath> ordered triples, all of which are, once again, clearly distinct from both the <imath>4</imath> triples and the <imath>6</imath> triples found above.


Hence, finally, the number of ordered triples <imath>(x,y,z)</imath> that will satisfy the system is <imath>27-4-6-6 = \boxed{\textbf{(C)}\ 11}</imath>.

~rionoh2

==Solution 3==

All equations are homogeneous linearly and symmetric. Therefore, we can approach via bounding.

<cmath>x+y+z \ge 2</cmath>
<cmath>-x+y+z \le 2</cmath>
<cmath>x-y+z \le 2</cmath>
<cmath>x+y-z \le 2</cmath>

We need to bound each of the inequalities. Begin by bounding <imath>z</imath> as <imath>z \le 2</imath>. Then, bound <imath>x</imath> as <imath>-x-y-z -x+y+z \le 0 \implies x \ge 0</imath>. Finally, bound <imath>y</imath> as <imath>y \le 2</imath>. By symmetry, one can find that <imath>x,y,z \ge 0, \le 2</imath>. We must have that <imath>x+y+z \ge 2, \le 6</imath>. Approach via minimalism.

If the minimum of the three integers is 0, WLOG say <imath>x</imath>, then we require <imath>y+z \ge 2, \le 6</imath>. That implies <imath>y = 2, z = 0; y=1, z =1, z = 0, y=2</imath> from which 3 cases arise. Due to symmetry, the cases <imath>(0,2), (2,0)</imath> are redundant, as I can let <imath>z = 0</imath> and obtain a similar result. Therefore, we have 2 viable cases in which 3 permutations so 6 total scenarios.

If the minimum of the three is 1, WLOG say <imath>x</imath>, then we require <imath>y+z \ge 1, \le 5</imath>. That implies <imath>y = 2, z = 1; y =1. z=1</imath>, which gives 3 and 1 case respectively, from which 4 cases.

If the minimum of the three is 2, WLOG say <imath>x</imath>, then we require <imath>y+z \ge 0, \le 4</imath> in which <imath>y=2, z=2</imath> is the only solution, giving 1 case.

The result is <imath>6+4+1 = \boxed{11}</imath>.

~Pinotation
